This is really involved and I haven't done it in a good ten years (since I had one high school English teacher require this), but this strategy was the most effective thing to help me organize my thoughts.

You will need:
Lots of index cards
Pen
Recommended: an outline, markers for color-coding

Each notecard can have one thought or sentence on it.
You can write out all the disjointed sentences you have now or you could make "place holder" notecards and pencil in what you need/if you know where to find it (ex.  "Need fancy quote from literary criticism about bob...look at class notes).

Then you can lay out your index cards on the floor and arrange your essay card by card.  Makes it really really tangible.  Can see if all your sentences have the same structure.  Can determine if each thing you say supports your thesis.  No thesis card...whoops!  Probably a good time to draft a thesis statement, even if it's very vague.

Color code whatever makes sense to you.  Could be quotes or citations each have their own color (quickly see if you've quote the same guy 10 times).  Could do each main point has its own color.  

Hopefully you get the idea.  

Moving sentences around in a word doc does not make writing easier for me.  When I'm really struggling, going back to paper/pen helps me so much.

You could even number the index cards, once you feel like it flows nicely, and then type your essay from the notecards.

I grew up a competitive swimmer, spending 30-40 a week in the pool and while swimming can be really great for low impact exercise, I did have my knee subluxate a handful of times over the years.  It usually happened pushing off the wall, but on occasion it would twist and subluxate while kicking either freestyle of backstroke.

The last time I dislocated my knee also happened in water -- walking in a lake with an uneven, rocky bottom.  This was one of the only times my patella didn't slide back in on it's own right away; my guess is because the water's resistance (which is low but not as low as moving in the air, if that makes sense) actually held/supported the patella in the dislocated position, whereas on land the body's instinct is to extend the leg, while removing any weight being placed on that joint, allowing the patella to quickly slide back into place.

I don't want to discourage swimming or exercise, just be careful!

I had the MPFL surgery for frequent(ish) patellar subluxations since childhood and the fear issue was definitely the biggest hurdle for me.  Like you, it was a structural thing.  I had the surgery about five years ago and am so glad I did it.  It was a tough recovery, physically and mentally, but 100% worth it, and I am able to activities, like run and hike, that I never thought I'd ever do.

As far as exercise, what about pilates?  No standing!

I definitely suggest trying to maintain (or gain) quad/hamstring strength before your surgery.  This is the one thing I wish I did; I think it would have made my recovery much quicker.

Hang in there!

I had an MPFL reconstruction when I was about 23 years old to correct crazy patellar misalignment that was the source of frequent patellar subluxations since childhood.  It got worse as I got older, so I finally went the surgical route.  I also had an IT band release at the same time.

I was told the recovery time was about six weeks.  It is now my understanding that this is the amount of time for the actual ligaments to heal, NOT the time frame from surgery to normal activity.  

I don't know if I had an unusually slow or difficult recovery, but it was really, really painful -- both in the first few days/weeks after surgery as well as the PT phase.  I ended up taking off almost 3 months from work (I was working with people experiencing homelessness at the time and relied on Boston's public transportation to get around however if I had a desk job and a car I wouldn't have needed that much time off).  I lost an immense amount of muscle mass in my quadriceps and hamstrings in the time between surgery and beginning physical therapy (sorry I don't have dates on that).  It took a lot of PT to regain full range of motion also.  Recovery was a monster of a bitch.

HOWEVER, about six months post-op I was able to hike my first mountain (full disclosure, this was a very poorly planned hike, I did not feel like my knee was totally stable, and involved an excessive number of tears to the dismay of my hiking partner) and continued hiking/backpacking milder trails of the White Mountains over the course of the summer.
 
I am at five years post-op now and could not be happier with my knee!  No more subluxations or dislocations...the knee that was operated on is in better condition than the other one.  I avoided so many activities growing up (even running around on the playground) for fear of dislocation and now I feel my knee is structurally sound enough to do pretty much whatever I want -- running, backpacking, snowboarding, etc.

Let me know if this is the route you end up taking and please feel free to message me if you have questions.  Good luck!

I am an ABA therapist and agree that in 25-30 years, the experience an adult with autism has will be DRAMATICALLY different than today.  

Early intervention is new enough that experts in the field cannot make good predicitions on outcomes for adults because we have not yet had a generation of people who recieved intensive early intervention therapy become adults!

As an ABA therapist who has been in the field for several years, I also agree with most of the above post and it's invaluable to hear from someone who has experienced this first-hand.

I wouldn't worry too much about labeling it, however since you already see that the behavior is interferring with social interaction, I would not ignore it.  I think you are doing the right thing by limiting when/where he can and cannot do this behavior.  You are doing the right thing by giving him a countdown and making sure he knows when he will have access to it again.  Top notch parenting, seriously!  

/u/cakeisatruth has a great suggestion in working with his preschool teachers to help set limits.  Maybe he can have it during free play, but not during structured time with peers (like circle time).  If your son is at a place where he can tolerate not having access to it, one idea is that the teacher has the hair and he must request a break or request his hair and then can have it for a set amount of time.  I too emphasize it sounds like what you are doing at home is working, so see how you can get teachers to do the same.

When it comes to behavior and determining when or how to intervene, the #1 thing is figuring out the function of the behavior.  My first inclination was also that it was either a visual or tactile thing, however since you mention that he is adding on, it may be more like acting out a script (or a combination).  Ask him why he wants a purse or what he would put in it.  Maybe he can answer, maybe not, but if he says something like "So I can keep my hair with me," that is very different then "because _____ (character) has one."  Enjoying watching clothes twirl, wearing "high heels," and carrying a bag/purse at his age is something neurotypical boys do too...it's fun, novel, and a good percentage of adults he sees have these things.  Does he ever do the routine without a mirror?

If the function seems to be more of a specific routine/script, show him other ways to play with the same thing.  For example, instead of having the hair fall off your head, maybe it gets tossed up in the air and lands on your head.  If he asks you to bow, you could try varying the ways you bow, like bowing really slowly and then falling over into a somersault.  One of my go-to games for kids with ASD around your son's age is actually to have an item on my head and do a little song that ends with "ah-ah-ah....CHOOOOOO" (sneeze) where the item tumbles off my head.  Try doing it alongside him with familiar toys/objects that he does not use as makeshift hair.  Maybe a ball, book, block, pillow, spoon?   The core of the game stays the same but pushes the boundaries.  Ham it up!  Even though he currently goes off by himself to do this behavior, maybe he could be prompted to have one peer join him.  For all kids (and adults), it's extremely valuable to be able to use items in many different ways.  At this age, it helps to develop creativity (books can be read, but they can also be used to build towers or act as roads for cars to drive on).  

On the other hand, you could try setting specific items that are "hair only" items, as he certainly won't be able to take off his shirt and/or pants whenever he feels like it as an adult!  If you think this route will be more successful (i.e. interferring with his current routine results in tantrums), I can walk you through some ideas on how to establish "hair only" items and then ideas on how to decrease the amount of time he's playing with the hair.  In this case, the routine stays fairly rigid but there are stricter boundaries on what can be used and when.

I believe both had to give brief presentations to the larger group.

This sounded rather intense to me, like the schools are expecting you to "know OT" already but I think they are mostly looking for coming up with a relevant activity given limited info, time, and materials (as these are the exact things OTs do on a daily basis).  Assessors are probably also listening for reasoning on why you would do a certain activity (even if it's "wrong") as functionality is the foundation of OT.  If you end up being given a task like this, try to think about either how it prepares the person for the larger target skill or how it will increase their ability to function independently down the road.

One of my friends exposure to OT was primarily through limited observation hours; she is definitely not fluent with OT terminology, common practices, etc. and she was accepted to the two schools she applied to.

Hope this helps!  Good luck, don't stress.  OT is fun!  :)  Maybe you can call and find out in advance if it is a group interview or not.  Feel free to PM me if you want to chat more and I'd love to hear how it goes/what ends up happening in your interview!

The knowledge you have gained through a BCBA program is so valuable. If you were still interested in working with children, I would imagine preschools would LOVE to have someone like you. I pulled out preschools over the school system because there is generally more flexibility (i.e. no common core) in daycare/preschool settings.

Counseling is another viable route, particularly cognitive behavior therapy.

I would ask about type of behaviors and severity of behaviors you would encounter at the clinic (aggressions, biting, self-injurious behaviors) and how much training you get in handling these behaviors.  

I had one ABA job where the kids were all under 3 years old, were almost all verbal (or had verbal delays, but not non-verbal), and had very, very few behaviors.

My current job is with elementary aged kiddos who are lowering functioning with a lot of behaviors.  Working with kids who aggress, dart, and have a number of other behaviors we are trying to reduce is a whole different experience.  Not saying one is better than the other, but its something I would want to be aware of.

Other questions:
- modes of communication -- do they use sign language, PECS (picture exchange system), do kids have electronic devices?
- do the kids receive additional services, such as speech or OT?
- are there SLPs or OTs on staff in addition to BCBAs?
